title: State and Local Vape Laws: Why the Rules Differ Where You Live
summary: Vape rules vary by state, county and city: licensing, flavor limits, taxes and where you can use them. Learn what to check before you order.
body:
Federal law sets a baseline for vapor products, but states, counties and cities add their own rules, and that is why a product that is available in one place may be restricted in another. For online buyers the differences matter a lot, because they decide what can lawfully be shipped to your address. This guide explains the main things that vary from place to place, why they affect online orders, how to check the rules where you live, what changes when you move or travel, how landlords and workplaces add their own limits and how we handle it. It is general information, not legal advice. Laws change and differ by state and city, so check the rules where you live. Everything we sell is for adults aged 21 and over, and nicotine is addictive.

## The federal baseline
Federal law sets the minimum age of 21 for buying tobacco products, including e-cigarettes, and sets rules for remote sales, such as adult signature on delivery and parcel labels. It also gives the FDA authority over the products. Those rules apply everywhere. States and local governments can add to them, but they cannot go below them. See [what 21+ age verification means](/blog/what-21-plus-age-verification-means/), [the PACT Act explained](/blog/pact-act-explained-for-vape-buyers/) and [the FDA and vaping products](/blog/fda-and-vaping-products-what-adults-should-know/).

## Things that vary
- **Flavor restrictions:** some states and cities limit or ban flavored vaping products, or allow only certain flavors such as tobacco.
- **Licensing:** sellers may need state or local licenses, and some places require them to be on an approved list.
- **Taxes:** many states tax vape products, in different ways, such as a percentage of price or an amount per milliliter.
- **Product authorization:** some states restrict sales to products that the FDA has authorized, or that appear on a state registry.
- **Usage rules:** where you can vape in public, in cars, in workplaces or near schools.
- **Packaging and quantity limits:** some places restrict package sizes, nicotine strengths or the number of units per sale.
- **Online sales:** some places restrict or ban shipments to residents.
- **Minimum age:** a few places set a higher minimum age than the federal 21.

## Why it affects online orders
We cannot ship where the law does not allow it, and we may cancel orders that cannot be delivered lawfully. A parcel sent to a place where a product is banned can be seized or returned, and the seller and the buyer could face penalties. That is why we are careful, and why we may contact you about an order. Read [where we ship and where we do not](/blog/where-we-ship-and-where-we-do-not/) for how this works in practice. If an order cannot be delivered lawfully, we cancel it and refund it through the payment method used.

## How to check your rules
Start with official sources. Look at your state health department or revenue department site, and your city or county's website. Search for "tobacco retail license", "flavored tobacco" and "vapor product tax" with your location. Check whether your state keeps a list of authorized products or approved retailers. Read the actual rule, not a summary, where you can, and look at the date, because rules change. If you are unsure whether we can ship a product to your area, ask us through the [contact page](/contact/) before you order, with your state and the product link.

### A quick method
1. Search for your state's rules on vapor products and flavors.
2. Search for your city or county's rules, which may be stricter.
3. Check whether the product you want is allowed where you live.
4. Check the minimum age and any limits on quantity or strength.
5. Ask us if you are still not sure.

## Taxes
Many states tax vapor products, and rates and methods differ. Some tax a percentage of the wholesale or retail price, others a fixed amount per unit or per milliliter. Sellers who ship to a state may need to register and collect the tax. Our [vape taxes by state overview](/blog/vape-taxes-by-state-overview/) explains the main approaches. Any tax that applies is shown in your order summary before you pay, so you always see the full amount.

## Moving or traveling
Rules change when you cross state lines. A product that is legal at home may be restricted where you are going, and vice versa. If you move, check the rules in your new location before you order. If you travel, check the rules at your destination, and read our guides on [traveling with vapes](/blog/traveling-with-vapes-airline-rules/) and [lithium battery care](/blog/lithium-battery-care-basics-for-vapes/). Do not ship products to an address in a place where they are not allowed.

## Landlords, workplaces and schools
Apartment buildings, employers and schools may ban vaping even where it is legal. A lease may forbid it, an employer may restrict it on premises and a school or campus may prohibit it entirely. Respect those rules, and be considerate of other people. Check your lease and your workplace policy, and keep devices and products stored responsibly, away from children and pets. See [adult vaper etiquette and responsibility](/blog/adult-vaper-etiquette-and-responsibility/).

## Cities and counties
Do not assume that state rules are the end of the story. Some cities and counties have rules that go further than the state's, such as flavor bans or licensing requirements. If you live in a large city, or a place that has recently changed its laws, check both the state and the local rules.

## Our commitment
We follow the rules that apply to us and expect customers to follow theirs. We ship only where the law allows, we require adult signature and we cancel orders that cannot be delivered lawfully. We cannot give legal advice, and we cannot track every local rule, so we rely on you to know yours and tell us if you are unsure. Read the [PACT Act overview](/blog/pact-act-explained-for-vape-buyers/) and our [terms](/terms/).

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### What if my state bans flavors?
Then flavored products cannot lawfully be shipped to you, and we may cancel an order that includes them. Ask us what is available for your area.

### What if the law changes after I order?
Contact us. We will tell you what we can do, which may include cancelling and refunding an order that can no longer be delivered lawfully.

### Can I order to a neighboring state's address?
Orders ship to the address where an adult will sign. The rules of the destination apply, not the rules of the buyer's home state, so check the destination.

### Do you collect sales or excise taxes?
Any tax that applies to your order is shown in your order summary. If you have questions about how taxes apply to you, contact us, and consult official sources.

### Are the rules the same for pouches and e-liquid?
Not always. Different products can be treated differently, so check the rules for the type of product you want.

## Not legal advice
This article is general information. It does not cover every rule, and rules change. For decisions that matter, check official sources and ask a qualified professional. Browse [disposable vapes](/shop/disposables/) only if you are 21 or older and the products are lawful where you live. All products are for adults aged 21 and over, and nicotine is addictive.

## A worked example: two customers, two outcomes
Customer A lives in a state with no flavor restrictions and an ordinary tax. They order a flavored disposable and a bottle of e-liquid. The order is checked, processed and shipped, and an adult signs for it. Customer B lives in a city that bans flavored vaping products. They order the same items. We contact them, explain that flavored products cannot lawfully be shipped to that address and offer to ship any items that are not restricted, or to cancel and refund the order. Customer B decides to cancel and is refunded through the payment method used. The difference is not about the customers; it is about the rules of the places they live.

## Keeping up with changes
Rules change often, through new laws, new regulations, court decisions and local ordinances. A rule you read a year ago may no longer apply. Check the date on any source, prefer official sources and check again before you place an order, especially if you live in a place that has recently been in the news for new vaping rules. If we learn of a change that affects your area, we will tell you.

## If you are a retailer
If you run a shop, the rules apply to you as a seller: licensing, taxes, age checks, displays, advertising and product lists. Check with your state and local authorities, and consider professional advice. Our [wholesale ordering guide](/blog/wholesale-ordering-guide/) explains what we need from retailers, and we supply registered businesses that can lawfully sell in their area.

## Frequently asked questions about checking rules
### Where is the best place to start?
Your state's official website, usually under health, revenue or tobacco control, followed by your city or county's site. Official pages are more reliable than summaries on social media.

### What if the rules look contradictory?
Local rules can be stricter than state rules, and both sit on top of federal rules. When they differ, the stricter rule applies. If you cannot tell, ask a qualified professional or the relevant authority.

### Can I rely on what a seller tells me about my local law?
Use it as a starting point only. A seller can tell you what it can ship, but you are responsible for knowing the rules where you live.

faq.q: Why do vape rules differ by state?
faq.a: Federal law sets a baseline, and states, counties and cities add their own rules on flavors, licensing, taxes, usage and online sales.

faq.q: Can you ship wherever I live?
faq.a: No. We cannot ship where the law does not allow it, and we may cancel orders that cannot be delivered lawfully.

faq.q: How do I check my local rules?
faq.a: Look at your state and city or county websites, search for tobacco retail license, flavored tobacco and vapor tax rules, and ask us if you are unsure.

faq.a: Yes. Many states tax vapor products in different ways. Any tax that applies is shown in your order summary.

faq.q: What if I move?
faq.a: Check the rules in your new location before you order, because they may differ.

faq.a: No. It is general information. Check official sources and ask a qualified professional.

title: Vape Taxes by State: A Plain Overview
summary: Many states tax vaping products, using different methods and rates. Here is how those taxes generally work and why they affect online orders.
body:
If your state taxes vaping products, the tax can change what you pay in a way that is easy to miss when you compare prices. Some states add a large percentage, some charge by the milliliter and some do not tax vapor products at all, so the same bottle or device can cost noticeably different amounts in different places. This guide explains why states tax vapor products, the main ways the tax is calculated, how online sales and the PACT Act fit in, how taxes show on an order with us, how the free-shipping threshold is measured, how to find exact figures for your state and how to compare real costs. It is general information, not legal advice. Laws change and differ by state and city, so check the rules where you live. Everything we sell is for adults aged 21 and over, and nicotine is addictive.

## Why states tax vapes
Many states levy excise taxes on e-cigarettes and e-liquids, similar to those on cigarettes. The goals vary. Some states want revenue, some want to discourage use, and some want to treat vapor products like other tobacco products for consistency. Because each state decides for itself, there is no single national vapor tax, and rates and methods differ widely. A few states have no specific vapor tax, while others charge rates that can double the price of a device.

## How taxes are calculated
Methods differ, and you may find more than one in a single state.

- **Percentage of price:** a share of the wholesale price or the retail price. A higher price means more tax, so premium devices cost more tax than economy ones.
- **Per milliliter:** a fixed amount for each milliliter of liquid. Larger bottles carry more tax, but the tax per milliliter stays the same.
- **Per device or per cartridge:** a flat amount per item, whatever its price.
- **Mixed systems:** a combination, such as a percentage on devices and a per-milliliter rate on liquids.
- **Different treatment of open and closed systems:** some states tax pre-filled disposables differently from refillable systems and bottles.

Because of those differences, you cannot guess a tax from the price alone. A $15 disposable and a $15 bottle can carry different amounts.

## Online sales and the PACT Act
Under the PACT Act, remote sellers must comply with state tax requirements, and in some cases collect and remit them. That means that when you buy online, a seller that follows the law handles the tax for the state where you live, or reports the sale to the state. See the [PACT Act overview](/blog/pact-act-explained-for-vape-buyers/). Some sellers cannot ship to certain states at all because the requirements are too complex, which is one reason availability differs by place. See [where we ship and where we do not](/blog/where-we-ship-and-where-we-do-not/).

## Seeing it on your order
Where a tax applies to an order, it is itemized in your order total, so you see it before you pay. Free-shipping thresholds are measured before tax, so tax does not push you over or under the line. Our free shipping applies to orders of $200 or more after discount and before tax. See [minimum order and free shipping explained](/blog/minimum-order-and-free-shipping-explained/). If you are unsure what a line on your summary means, contact us before you pay.

## Where to get exact numbers
Rates change often, and the exact rules depend on the product type and your location. Check your state's department of revenue or taxation website for current rules, and search for "vapor product tax" or "e-cigarette tax" with your state's name. Look at the date of any page you use, because older pages may be out of date. Some cities and counties add their own taxes on top of the state's. Official sources are more reliable than summaries on social media or in forums.

## Impact on prices
Tax can raise the cost of a vape noticeably in some states. A device that looks cheap before tax can cost much more after it, and a larger bottle can carry a larger tax even if the price per milliliter is low. When you compare costs between products or between sellers, compare the final total, including tax and shipping, not just the sticker price. Compare overall costs with [cost per puff](/blog/how-to-compare-vape-prices-per-puff/), and remember that bulk purchases can lower both shipping and cost per item. See [bulk buying tips](/blog/bulk-buying-vapes-save-money/).

### A worked example with round numbers
Suppose a state charges a 20% tax on the retail price of vapor products. A $20 disposable would carry $4.00 of tax, for $24.00. A $100 order of mixed products would carry $20.00, for $120.00. If your state instead charged $0.10 per milliliter of liquid, a 30 mL bottle would carry $3.00, and a 100 mL bottle $10.00, regardless of the sticker price. These figures are only illustrations. The actual rate for your state is on your state's website, and any tax that applies is shown in your order summary before you pay.

## Taxes and the 10% discount
The 10% discount for cryptocurrency and gift cards applies to the product subtotal. How tax interacts with a discount depends on the state's rules, which may tax the discounted price or the original price. Your order summary shows the figures that apply to your order. If you are close to a threshold or comparing totals, check the summary for each payment method.

## Wholesale buyers
Retailers have their own obligations, such as licenses, tax registration and stamps, which may differ from the rules for individuals. If you buy wholesale, check with your state's tax authority about what applies to your business, and see our [wholesale ordering guide](/blog/wholesale-ordering-guide/). We supply registered businesses, and they are responsible for compliance with their own tax rules.

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Why does the tax differ between products?
Because states tax by price, by volume or by item, and some treat disposables, bottles and devices differently.

### Will you add tax to my order?
Where a tax applies to your order, it is itemized in your order total before you pay. If you have questions about how tax appears on your order, contact us with your state.

### Can I avoid vape tax?
Taxes are set by law, and a seller that follows the law cannot skip them. Be cautious of sellers that offer to avoid tax, because that may mean they are not complying with the rules, which can put your order at risk.

### Do taxes change often?
Yes. States change rates and methods from time to time. Check official sources before a large purchase.

### Does tax affect returns?
Refunds are based on what you paid for the returned item, and any tax paid on it is handled according to the rules that apply. We explain the details when we arrange a return. See [refund and return policy explained](/blog/refund-and-return-policy-explained/).

## Questions
Contact us through the [contact page](/contact/) with your state and we will explain how it appears on your order. Browse [vape juice](/shop/vape-juice/) and [disposable vapes](/shop/disposables/). All products are for adults aged 21 and over, and nicotine is addictive.

## Frequently asked questions about tax on your order
### Why do two customers pay different tax for the same product?
Because tax depends on where the parcel is going. A product shipped to a state with a percentage tax carries more tax than one shipped to a state with none, and a state that taxes by the milliliter charges more on a large bottle.

### Is the tax part of the price I see on the product page?
The product page shows the price of the product. Where a tax applies to your order, it is itemized in your order summary, so you see the full amount before you pay.

### Do taxes apply to accessories and parts?
It depends on the state. Some tax devices and accessories as well as liquids, and some do not. If you are unsure, ask us with your state.

## Keeping records
If you are a business or you track your spending, keep your order confirmation and invoice, which show the items, the totals and any tax. For a retailer, these records support your own tax filings. For an individual, they are simply a record of what you paid. If you need an invoice in a particular format, ask us.

## Staying informed
State tax rules are updated through legislation and regulation, and the details are published by state revenue departments. If you buy regularly, check your state's page once or twice a year, and again when you hear of a change. Being aware of changes helps you plan larger orders and avoid surprises.

## A short checklist before a larger order
1. Find your state's rule on vapor products and note whether it taxes by price, volume or item.
2. Check your order summary for any tax line before you pay.
3. Compare totals for each payment method, including any discount.
4. Keep the invoice for your records.
5. Contact us with your state if a line on the summary is unclear.

Five minutes of checking is cheaper than a surprise at the end of the process.

title: Traveling With Vapes: Airline and Battery Rules in Brief
summary: Vapes belong in carry-on bags, never checked luggage, and cannot be used on board. Learn the basics before your next trip.
body:
Traveling with a vape is simple once you know the handful of rules that apply almost everywhere, and a headache if you find them out at the airport. Devices, batteries and liquids are all treated differently from ordinary luggage, the rules at your destination can be very different from the rules at home, and a few small habits make a big difference to whether your trip goes smoothly. This guide covers where devices and batteries must travel, why vaping on board is prohibited, how to protect batteries, how the liquid rules work, what to check about your destination and about international travel, how to pack and what to do if something goes wrong. It is general information, not legal advice. Laws and airline policies change and differ by state, city, airline and country, so check the rules that apply to your trip. Everything we sell is for adults aged 21 and over, and nicotine is addictive.

## Carry-on only
Under U.S. aviation rules, e-cigarettes, vaporizers and spare lithium batteries must travel in carry-on baggage. They are not allowed in checked bags, because a battery fire is much easier to detect and handle in the cabin than in a cargo hold. This applies to devices with built-in batteries, such as disposables and pod kits, as well as to loose spare cells for box mods. If you arrive at the airport with a vape in a bag you intend to check, you will need to move it to your carry-on before you go through the checkpoint. Airlines and security officers can require this, and a device found in a checked bag may be removed.

### Why the rule exists
Lithium batteries can overheat if they are damaged or short-circuited. In the cabin, crew can respond quickly. In the hold, a fire could go unnoticed for longer. That is the reasoning behind the same rule for power banks and many other battery-powered devices.

## No vaping on board
Using a vape on a commercial aircraft, including in the lavatory, is prohibited. This applies to every flight, and it includes charging a vape from the aircraft's power outlets in some cases, depending on the airline's rules. Do not use or charge your device during a flight unless the airline explicitly permits charging, and even then keep it supervised. Violations can bring fines, and crews take them seriously. Plan ahead for long flights, including how you will manage without vaping, and avoid using your device in the terminal where it is not allowed.

## Protect batteries
Battery protection is the most useful habit for travel.

- **Keep spare batteries in a case** or in separate pouches so that metal objects, such as keys and coins, cannot touch the terminals.
- **Switch off devices** before you pack them, and lock the fire button if it has a lock function.
- **Store them where they cannot be pressed accidentally,** for example in a small zipped pocket, not loose at the bottom of a bag.
- **Do not pack a damaged device.** A swollen, dented or hot device should not travel at all. See [lithium battery care basics](/blog/lithium-battery-care-basics-for-vapes/).
- **Keep devices out of heat** such as a hot car or direct sun on the way to the airport.
- **Keep it accessible.** A device in an outer pocket or a small pouch is easy to show to a security officer if asked.

## Liquids
Liquids follow the standard carry-on liquid rules in most places: containers of 3.4 ounces (100 milliliters) or less, in a single clear resealable bag, with larger bottles not permitted in carry-on. Pressure changes during a flight can cause leaks, so use pods that are nearly empty or sealed, tighten caps, and put bottles in a sealed bag in case they leak. Do not fill a tank just before a flight, because expanding air can push liquid out. If you use refillable devices, consider traveling with a small bottle and filling after you land. See [choosing a vape for travel](/blog/best-vapes-for-travel/) for devices that suit trips.

### Disposables as travel devices
Many travelers choose disposables because they are sealed and need no liquid handling. They still contain a battery, so they must travel in carry-on. A smaller device packs more easily and is less likely to leak, but check that it is not damaged before you travel.

## At security
Be ready to show your device at security. Officers may ask you to remove vapes and batteries from your bag, and they may inspect them. Keep them accessible, answer questions politely and follow instructions. If an officer says a device cannot travel, accept it and ask what the options are. You are responsible for what is in your bag, so know what you are carrying.

## At your destination
Rules differ by state, city and country. Some places ban vape use in public places, workplaces, hotels, rental cars and parks, and a few restrict possession or sales. A hotel can charge a cleaning fee for vaping in a room. Check the rules before you travel, and read our overview of [state and local vape laws](/blog/state-and-local-vape-laws-explained/). Respect no-vaping signs, and be considerate of other people.

### Shipping to your destination
If you will be away from home for a while, remember that deliveries need an adult to sign. Do not ship a parcel to a hotel or a short-term rental unless you are sure an adult aged 21 or older will receive it with ID. See [shipping address tips](/blog/shipping-address-tips/).

## International travel
Many countries restrict or ban vapes and nicotine liquids, and some impose heavy penalties for carrying them. A device that is legal at home can be illegal to import. Check the laws and customs rules of every country you will pass through, including transit stops, before you go. If a country bans nicotine liquid, do not carry it. If you are unsure, consider leaving your device at home. The consequences of getting this wrong, including fines and confiscation, are not worth the convenience.

## Packing checklist
1. Device switched off, with any lock engaged.
2. Spare batteries in a case.
3. Device and batteries in your carry-on, not your checked bag.
4. Liquids in small, sealed containers within the carry-on limit.
5. Cap tight and pods nearly empty or sealed.
6. Everything in a place that is easy to reach at security.
7. A plan for where you can vape legally at your destination.

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Can I vape in the airport?
Only in areas where it is permitted. Many airports ban it in the terminal, and some have designated smoking areas. Check signs, and do not vape in restrooms.

### Can I charge my vape on the plane?
Airlines differ, and many discourage or prohibit charging devices that are not specifically allowed. Do not charge unattended, and follow crew instructions. Better still, charge before you go and carry a charged device.

### Do I need to declare my vape?
You do not usually need to declare it, but you must put it in your carry-on, and you may be asked about it at security.

### What if my device is confiscated?
Ask the officer about the options, such as handing it to someone who is not traveling. Do not argue, and do not try to hide it.

### Can I bring nicotine pouches?
Pouches are not batteries or liquids, so they are not covered by the same rules, but other countries restrict them heavily, and some states do too. Check your destination.

## Related
Check [battery care basics](/blog/lithium-battery-care-basics-for-vapes/), [how to dispose of vapes and batteries](/blog/how-to-dispose-of-vapes-and-batteries/) and [state and local vape laws](/blog/state-and-local-vape-laws-explained/). Browse [vape kits](/shop/vape-kits/) and [disposable vapes](/shop/disposables/). All products are for adults aged 21 and over, and nicotine is addictive.

## A worked example: a weekend trip
You are flying from Phoenix to Chicago for a long weekend with a pod kit, two spare pods and a small bottle of liquid. At home you check that the kit is charged, switch it off and lock the button. You put the device and the pods in a zipped pocket of your carry-on, and the liquid in a clear bag with your other toiletries, in a bottle under 3.4 ounces. At security you take the bag out if asked, show the device and put it back. On the plane you do not use it. In Chicago you check the local rules before you vape outdoors, and you avoid using it in the hotel room. On the return flight, you pack everything the same way. The whole routine takes five minutes, and nothing about it is complicated once you have done it.

## If you are connecting through other countries
If your route passes through another country, even only for a layover, its rules apply while you are there. Some countries inspect baggage in transit, and a device that is banned there can be confiscated or lead to penalties. Check the rules for every stop, and if you are in doubt, travel without the device. For flights within the United States, the main rules are the carry-on requirement and the ban on use on board, but the airline's own policy may add more, so read it before you fly.

## Tips for frequent travelers
Keep a small travel kit that stays packed: a spare battery case, a clear bag for liquids and a lanyard or pouch for the device. Replace anything that is worn. Check your device before each trip for swelling, damage or a loose cap. Buy a travel-size bottle rather than decanting from a large one at the airport. And do not rely on being able to buy a replacement at your destination, because rules and availability differ.

faq.q: Can I put my vape in checked luggage?
faq.a: No. Under U.S. aviation rules, e-cigarettes, vaporizers and spare lithium batteries must travel in carry-on baggage.

faq.q: Can I vape on a plane?
faq.a: No. Using a vape on a commercial aircraft, including in the lavatory, is prohibited.

faq.q: How should I pack spare batteries?
faq.a: In a case or separate pouches so metal objects cannot touch the terminals, with devices switched off and the fire button locked if it has a lock.

faq.q: What are the liquid limits?
faq.a: Standard carry-on rules apply: containers of 3.4 ounces (100 milliliters) or less in a clear resealable bag. Keep pods nearly empty or sealed to avoid leaks.

faq.q: Can I take a vape abroad?
faq.a: Many countries restrict or ban vapes and nicotine liquids. Check the laws and customs rules of every country on your route before you go.

faq.q: What if my destination bans vaping?
faq.a: Respect the rules. Some places ban use in public, hotels and rental cars, or restrict possession.

title: Lithium Battery Care Basics for Vape Devices
summary: Most vapes use lithium-ion batteries. Follow these care basics to protect the device, avoid damage and extend battery life.
body:
Almost every rechargeable vape uses a lithium-ion battery, the same type that powers phones, laptops and power banks. These batteries are reliable when they are treated well and can fail badly when they are damaged, overheated or misused, which is why a few simple habits matter so much. This guide explains how to use the right charger, why not to leave a device charging unattended, how heat and cold affect batteries, how to recognize a damaged device, how to carry devices without risk of a short circuit, what is different about replaceable batteries, how to build good charging habits and when to stop using a device altogether. It is general information for adults aged 21 and over, not a substitute for the manufacturer's instructions. Nicotine is addictive.

## How a lithium-ion battery works, briefly
A lithium-ion battery stores energy by moving lithium ions between two electrodes. It is compact and powerful, which is why it suits small devices. But it also holds a lot of energy in a small space, and if the internal parts are damaged or the battery is overheated or overcharged, that energy can be released quickly as heat, which is the source of the rare but serious battery fires that make the news. Good habits keep the battery in the range where it behaves as designed.

## Use the right charger
Charge with the cable supplied or a reputable one, from a standard USB port or wall adapter. Cheap, unbranded chargers can supply inconsistent power and may lack the protections that quality chargers include. If your device has a USB-C port, use a good USB-C cable, and avoid frayed or bent connectors. If a cable or a port is damaged, replace it. Do not use a charger with a much higher power rating than the device expects unless the manufacturer says it is supported. See [how to charge a disposable](/blog/how-to-charge-a-disposable/).

## Do not leave it charging unattended
Charge on a hard, flat, non-flammable surface, such as a table or a countertop, and avoid sleeping with a charging device by your bed or on soft furnishings. Do not charge under a pillow, on a sofa or in a bag. Stay in the room while it charges, and unplug it when it is full. A device that charges overnight every night is exposed to more risk than one that charges in daylight under your eye.

## Avoid heat and cold
Do not leave a vape in a hot car or direct sun, and avoid freezing temperatures. Heat shortens battery life and can damage the device. Cold reduces performance temporarily and can harm a battery if you charge it while it is very cold. Let a device return to room temperature before you charge or use it. Keep devices away from radiators, heaters and sunny windowsills. If a device feels hot while charging or using, stop and unplug it.

## Do not use a damaged device
Stop using any device that is swollen, dented, hot to touch, leaking or has damaged wiring. A swollen casing can mean that the battery is failing. Do not charge it, do not carry it in a pocket and do not try to repair or open it. Move it to a hard surface away from anything flammable, and dispose of it properly; see [how to dispose of vapes and batteries](/blog/how-to-dispose-of-vapes-and-batteries/). If a device ever smokes or becomes very hot, move away from it and call emergency services if there is a fire risk.

## Pocket and bag habits
Keep devices separate from coins and keys, which can short the battery terminals or press the fire button. Use a case if possible, and carry spare batteries in a proper case rather than loose. Avoid carrying a device in a back pocket, where sitting on it can bend it. For travel, follow the rules in [traveling with vapes](/blog/traveling-with-vapes-airline-rules/).

## Replaceable batteries
Box mods that use removable cells need correctly rated batteries from a reputable source. Never mix brands, ages or charge levels in the same device. Use cells whose wraps are in good condition, and replace any with tears or exposed metal. Check that the battery's current rating suits the device, because a battery that cannot supply enough current can overheat. Charge cells in a proper external charger on a hard surface, and never leave them charging unattended.

## Charging habits
Charge before the device is completely empty when you can, and unplug once it is full. Lithium-ion batteries last longer if they are not regularly run to zero or kept at a full charge for days. A partial top-up is fine. If you will not use a device for a long time, store it partly charged in a cool, dry place. See [extending battery life](/blog/how-to-extend-vape-battery-life/).

### Disposables with rechargeable batteries
Many large-capacity disposables have USB-C ports. Charge them as you would any small device, and do not keep charging them after they stop working, which can be a sign that the liquid is finished but the battery still holds a charge.

## Signs a battery is nearing the end
- The device runs out of charge much faster than it used to.
- It takes much longer to charge, or does not reach full.
- The casing feels warm even when idle.
- The device turns off by itself.
- There is any swelling, odor or leaking.

If you see any of these, retire the device. A new one costs far less than the risk.

## What to do in an emergency
If a battery starts to smoke or burn, do not touch it with bare hands. If you can do so without risk, move away from flammable items and call emergency services. Do not use water on a lithium battery fire unless instructed by emergency services; keep people and pets away. Afterward, do not use the device, and dispose of it as hazardous waste.

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Is it a problem to charge overnight?
It is better not to. If you do, use a hard, flat, non-flammable surface, a quality charger and a device in good condition, and never charge a damaged device.

### Can I use a phone charger?
Usually yes, if it is a reputable USB charger and the device uses a standard cable. Avoid very high-power fast chargers unless the manufacturer says they are supported.

### Why does my device get warm?
Slight warmth during charging or heavy use is normal. Hot to touch is not, and you should stop using it.

### How long do batteries last?
It depends on the device and how you use it. A battery that is looked after lasts longer, but eventually every battery wears out.

### Can I recycle a battery myself?
Take devices and batteries to a hazardous waste or electronics recycling site. Do not put them in household trash or curbside recycling.

## Where to shop
Browse [vape kits](/shop/vape-kits/) and [disposable vapes](/shop/disposables/). Read the instructions that come with your device. All products are for adults aged 21 and over, and nicotine is addictive.

## A weekly habit check
Once a week, look at your device. Check the casing for dents, swelling or cracks. Check the charging port for bent pins or debris. Check the cable for fraying. Check that the device is not unusually warm when idle. Wipe the outside with a dry cloth. It takes a minute, and it catches problems before they become serious. If you carry spare batteries, check the wraps and the case at the same time.

## What to do with an old device
When a device reaches the end of its life, stop using it and take it for recycling instead of leaving it in a drawer. An old battery that is left unattended can degrade further. Follow the guidance in [how to dispose of vapes and batteries](/blog/how-to-dispose-of-vapes-and-batteries/). If you are replacing a device, choose one with a reputable battery and a standard charging port, and read the manufacturer's instructions before first use.

## Myths about batteries
- **"You must drain a battery before charging."** Modern lithium-ion batteries do not need it, and frequent full drains can shorten their life.
- **"Any charger is fine."** Poor chargers can damage batteries and are a common cause of problems.
- **"A warm battery is normal."** Slight warmth is normal. Hot to touch is not.
- **"A swollen battery is still usable."** It is not. Stop using it at once.

Knowing the facts helps you keep your devices working and reduces the chance of an incident.

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Is it normal for a disposable to stop working before the liquid is gone?
It can happen. Heavy use, heat and cold all reduce battery life, and a non-rechargeable device may stop when the battery is spent. Do not try to open it. Take it for recycling.

### Can I use a vape while it is charging?
It is better not to. Using a device while it charges makes it hotter, and some devices are not designed for it. Unplug it, then use it.

### Should I keep spare batteries in the fridge?
No. Store them at room temperature in a case, away from heat and moisture.

### What if I drop my device?
Check it for dents and cracks. If it is damaged, or if it feels warm or smells odd afterward, stop using it and dispose of it properly.

faq.q: What charger should I use?
faq.a: The cable supplied or a reputable one, from a standard USB port or wall adapter. Cheap, unbranded chargers can supply inconsistent power.

faq.q: Can I charge overnight?
faq.a: It is better not to. Charge on a hard, flat, non-flammable surface, stay nearby and unplug when full.

faq.q: How does heat affect a vape?
faq.a: Heat shortens battery life and can damage the device. Do not leave a vape in a hot car or direct sun.

faq.q: When should I stop using a device?
faq.a: If it is swollen, dented, hot to touch, leaking or has damaged wiring. Do not charge it, and dispose of it properly.

faq.q: How should I carry a vape?
faq.a: Away from coins and keys that could short the terminals or press the fire button, ideally in a case.

faq.q: What about removable batteries?
faq.a: Use correctly rated cells from a reputable source, never mix brands, ages or charge levels, and replace any with damaged wraps.

title: How to Dispose of Vapes, Pods and Batteries Responsibly
summary: Vapes contain batteries, electronics and residual nicotine. Here is how to dispose of them properly and where to look for recycling options.
body:
A used vape is not ordinary trash. It contains a lithium battery, electronics, plastics and residual liquid containing nicotine, and each of those needs different handling. Throwing a device in the household bin or the curbside recycling can start fires in garbage trucks and recycling plants, and leaking liquid is hazardous to children, pets and the environment. This guide explains why disposal matters, why not to use household trash or curbside recycling, where to take vapes and batteries, how to prepare a device for drop-off, what to do with liquids, pods and coils, how to deal with damaged devices and how to reduce waste in the first place. It is general information for adults aged 21 and over, and local rules differ, so check yours. Nicotine is addictive.

## Why it matters
Lithium batteries can start fires when they are crushed or punctured, which can happen in garbage trucks, compactors and recycling plants. Such fires are a real risk to workers and facilities, and they are a reason many municipalities have specific rules. Nicotine liquid is hazardous to children, pets and wildlife if it leaks, and it should not enter drains or soil. Devices also contain metals and plastics that can be recovered when they are recycled properly. Responsible disposal is part of being an adult user.

## Do not put them in household trash or curbside recycling
Many municipalities treat vapes as electronic or hazardous waste, and put them on the list of items that must not go in household bins. Even where rules are relaxed, a lithium battery in a bin is a fire risk. Check your local rules on your city or county waste page, and follow them. If you are unsure, treat the device as hazardous waste.

## Where to take them
- **Household hazardous waste sites** and collection events, which accept batteries, electronics and liquids.
- **Electronics recycling programs** that accept small electronics, including some retail take-back programs.
- **Battery drop-off locations** at some retailers, which may accept lithium batteries, sometimes only certain types or sizes.
- **Municipal collection days** for bulky or electronic waste.

Search for your city's hazardous waste page, or use a recycling locator that lets you search by item and location. Call ahead if you are unsure whether a site accepts vapes, because acceptance varies.

## Before you drop it off
Stop using any damaged or swollen device. Put it in a sealed plastic bag, tape over any exposed battery terminals, and keep it away from heat and flammable items. Do not try to open, crush or puncture it, and do not try to remove the battery from a disposable. Keep it out of reach of children and pets until you can take it. If the device is leaking, double-bag it, wear gloves and wash your hands afterward.

### Small steps that reduce risk
- Store used devices in a cool, dry place in a container, not loose in a drawer.
- Do not stack many devices together with exposed terminals.
- Take devices for recycling promptly, instead of letting them build up.

## Liquids
Do not pour leftover liquid down the drain or onto the ground. Absorb small amounts with cat litter or paper towels, seal in a bag and take it to hazardous waste, following local guidance. For unused bottles you no longer want, ask your hazardous waste site what they accept. Keep bottles capped and out of reach of children and pets until you can take them, as explained in [keeping vapes and e-liquid away from children and pets](/blog/keeping-vapes-away-from-children-and-pets/).

## Pods and coils
Used pods and coils go in the same stream as the device, unless your local program says otherwise. They contain residue, and some contain small metal parts. Collect them in a sealed bag and take them with your device. Do not rinse them down the sink.

## Nicotine pouches
Used pouches are small, but they still contain nicotine residue and should not be left where children or pets can reach them. Dispose of them in a bin with a lid, or follow local guidance. Empty cans are usually recyclable where your local program accepts that kind of container, but check the rules. See [how to store nicotine pouches](/blog/how-to-store-nicotine-pouches/).

## Packaging
Cartons and padding from your order are ordinary materials and can usually go in recycling. Remove address labels if you prefer. Keep any original packaging for a short while if you might return an item. See [discreet packaging](/blog/discreet-packaging-what-to-expect/).

## Reducing waste
- **Choose rechargeable devices** that you can use for longer, and consider refillable systems if they suit you.
- **Match the product to your use,** so you do not throw away large amounts of unused product.
- **Avoid stockpiling** more than you will use, because old products can degrade.
- **Take devices for recycling** instead of throwing them away.
- **Buy replacement parts** such as pods and coils instead of replacing a whole device, where your device supports it.

See [rechargeable vs non-rechargeable disposables](/blog/rechargeable-vs-non-rechargeable-disposables/) and [how to pick replacement coils and pods](/blog/how-to-pick-replacement-coils-and-pods/).

## What if there is a fire or smoke?
If a battery smokes, gets very hot or catches fire, do not touch it with bare hands. If it is possible to do so without risk, move flammable items away, and call emergency services. Keep people and pets away. Afterward, treat the device as hazardous waste. See [lithium battery care basics](/blog/lithium-battery-care-basics-for-vapes/).

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Can I put a vape in the regular bin if there is no recycling nearby?
It is not recommended, because of the fire risk. Look for the nearest hazardous waste site, or ask your city about collection options.

### Can I mail a used vape back to you?
We do not accept used devices through the returns process. Our returns policy covers unopened items. Dispose of used devices locally.

### What about empty bottles?
Empty bottles still contain residue. Check with your local hazardous waste program, and keep them out of reach until you dispose of them.

### Are disposables recyclable?
The battery and electronics can be recycled at the right facility. The device as a whole should go to electronics or hazardous waste recycling, not household recycling.

### How do I find a recycling site?
Search your city or county's waste page, or use a recycling locator for electronics and batteries.

## Related
Learn about [battery care](/blog/lithium-battery-care-basics-for-vapes/) and [keeping vapes away from children and pets](/blog/keeping-vapes-away-from-children-and-pets/). Browse [disposable vapes](/shop/disposables/). All products are for adults aged 21 and over, and nicotine is addictive.

## A worked example: clearing out a drawer
You find five finished disposables in a drawer, two with scuffed casings. You put on gloves, check that none is swollen or hot, and place them in a sealed plastic bag, with tape over the charging ports of the scuffed ones. You search your city's website for "household hazardous waste", find a drop-off site that accepts small electronics and batteries and note its hours. You also gather two empty bottles and a used pod, bag them separately and bring everything on Saturday morning. At the site, you tell the attendant what you have, and they take it. The whole task takes less than an hour, and the drawer is clear.

## Common mistakes
- **Putting devices in the bin** because they look like plastic.
- **Leaving finished devices lying around,** where children or pets might find them.
- **Crushing or opening a device** to remove the battery.
- **Pouring liquid down the sink.**
- **Stacking devices together** with exposed terminals.

Avoiding these keeps you, your household and waste workers out of harm's way. If you make one of them by mistake, move the item to a hard surface away from flammable items, and call your local waste authority for advice.

## A note for retailers
If you run a shop, you may have additional obligations for handling and disposing of returned or expired stock. Check with your local authorities and a licensed waste handler. Do not mix vapor products with general trade waste.

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Can I bring many devices at once?
Many sites accept household quantities. If you have a large number, call first, because there may be limits per visit.

### Do I have to remove the battery?
No, and you should not try. Take the whole device. Removing a battery from a sealed device can damage it and cause a fire.

### Is there a cost?
Many household hazardous waste programs are free for residents. Retail take-back programs are often free too. Check with the site.

### What if I cannot find a site nearby?
Contact your city or county waste department, or ask a local electronics retailer. Until you can take the items, store them in a sealed bag in a cool place, out of reach of children and pets.

## Planning disposal as part of your routine
The easiest way to dispose of devices responsibly is to make it a routine instead of a chore. Keep a small lidded container in a high place for finished devices and pods. When it is half full, take it to a drop-off site on a day when you are already out, such as when you shop or run errands. Note the dates of local collection events on a calendar. If you live with other adults who use these products, agree who takes the container. A routine means that finished devices never pile up, and that nothing is left lying around.

## Why it is worth the effort
Each device you recycle keeps a lithium battery out of the waste stream and returns materials to use. It also keeps nicotine residue away from children, pets and water. The effort is small compared with the risk of a fire in a bin or a collection truck, and compared with the harm a leaking bottle can do. Responsible disposal is one of the simplest ways to be a considerate adult user.

### What the process looks like at a drop-off site
You arrive, tell an attendant what you have and hand over the sealed bag or place it where they direct. The attendant sorts it into the correct stream. You do not need to explain how you used it, and you are not judged for using it. The aim is to get the items out of circulation securely and responsibly.

faq.q: Can I throw a vape in the trash?
faq.a: No. A vape contains a lithium battery, electronics and nicotine residue. Take it to hazardous waste or electronics recycling.

faq.q: Where can I take used vapes?
faq.a: Household hazardous waste sites and events, electronics recycling programs and some battery drop-off locations. Check your local rules.

faq.q: How should I prepare a device for drop-off?
faq.a: Put it in a sealed bag, tape over exposed terminals, keep it away from heat and do not open or crush it.

faq.q: What do I do with leftover liquid?
faq.a: Do not pour it down the drain. Absorb small amounts with cat litter or paper towels, seal in a bag and take it to hazardous waste.

faq.q: What about used pods and coils?
faq.a: They go in the same stream as the device unless your local program says otherwise.

faq.q: Can I return used devices to you?
faq.a: No. Our returns policy covers unopened items only. Dispose of used devices locally.

title: Keeping Vapes and E-Liquid Away From Children and Pets
summary: Nicotine liquid and devices must be kept out of reach. Here is how adults can store them responsibly and what to do if there is a spill.
body:
E-liquid contains nicotine, and a small amount can be dangerous to children and pets. Brightly colored packaging, fruit flavors and small, easy-to-open parts make these products attractive to curious hands and noses, which is why responsible storage is part of being an adult user. This guide explains how to store liquids, pods, pouches and devices out of reach, why original packaging matters, what to avoid, how to handle spills, what to do if someone is exposed, how to dispose of products responsibly and everyday habits that keep your home secure. It is general information for adults aged 21 and over and is not medical advice. If you think a child or pet has been exposed to nicotine, contact Poison Control or emergency services immediately.

## Why it matters
Nicotine is a potent substance. Children and small pets can be affected by amounts that would hardly register for an adult, and a single bottle contains a large quantity. Liquids can be swallowed or absorbed through the skin, and pouches, which look like candy to some children, are another risk. Devices contain batteries and small parts that can also cause harm. Prevention is the best protection, and it takes only a few habits.

## Store out of reach and out of sight
Keep liquids, pods, pouches and devices in a high, closed cabinet or a lockable box. Do not leave them on tables, counters, in handbags, in coat pockets or in cars where children or pets can reach them. Remember that children can climb, and that pets can open soft bags. A lockable box is worth the small cost, because it keeps working even when you forget. Put products away after each use, and do not leave them on a charger within reach.

### Where not to store
- **On coffee tables or bedside tables.**
- **In open bags or backpacks** that children can reach.
- **In drawers without locks** that a child can open.
- **In cars,** where heat also damages products.
- **Near food** or in the kitchen, where children look for snacks.

## Keep original packaging
Child-resistant caps and warning labels are on the packaging for a reason. Keep products in their original containers with the labels, so that anyone who finds them knows what they are, and so that poison control can identify the contents if there is an emergency. Do not decant liquid into unlabelled bottles or food-style containers. Keep the caps tight, and make sure child-resistant mechanisms click fully shut.

## Do not use food-style containers
Brightly colored or fruit-flavored liquid can attract attention. Never store it in drink bottles, jars or near snacks, because a child could mistake it for a drink. Keep it away from where food and drink are kept. The same goes for pouches: keep the can closed and out of reach, and do not leave loose pouches anywhere.

## Handle spills promptly
Wipe spills with paper towels while wearing gloves, wash the surface and your hands, and dispose of the towels responsibly. Avoid skin contact, and keep children and pets away until you have finished. If liquid gets on your skin, wash it off with soap and water straight away. If it gets in your eyes, rinse with water and seek advice. Clean up before you do anything else, because a spill on a floor can be reached by a crawling child or a pet.

## If someone is exposed
Contact Poison Control right away at 1-800-222-1222 in the U.S., or your local emergency number if the person is unwell. Do not wait for symptoms. Have the product's packaging or the label to hand so that you can tell them what it is and how much may have been taken. For pets, contact a veterinarian or an animal poison control service at once. Do not try to make anyone vomit unless a professional tells you to. Quick action matters.

### What to have ready
- The product packaging or a photo of the label.
- The approximate amount involved and when it happened.
- The age and weight of the person or pet.

## Dispose responsibly
Used devices, empty pods and used pouches are also hazardous. Keep them out of reach until you dispose of them, and follow the rules in [how to dispose of vapes and batteries](/blog/how-to-dispose-of-vapes-and-batteries/). Do not put them in an open bin where a child or pet could reach them.

## Everyday habits
- **Charge devices where children cannot reach them,** and never leave them charging unattended.
- **Never let anyone under 21 handle a vape.** Read about [age verification](/blog/what-21-plus-age-verification-means/).
- **Do not vape around children or pets,** and keep vapor away from their faces.
- **Tell visitors** where products are stored and to keep their own bags closed.
- **Check regularly** that nothing has been left lying around, especially after guests.
- **Teach older children** that these products are for adults only and are not toys.

See [how to store e-liquid](/blog/how-to-store-e-liquid/) and [how to store disposable vapes](/blog/how-to-store-disposable-vapes/).

## Special situations
### When you have visitors
Visitors may bring children and pets who are not used to your home. Put products away before they arrive, and keep them away while they stay.

### When you travel
Keep products in a closed bag that you control. Do not leave them in hotel rooms where cleaners or other guests might find them. See [traveling with vapes](/blog/traveling-with-vapes-airline-rules/).

### When you move
Pack products separately, keep them with you and unpack them into a secure place straight away.

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Are some products more dangerous than others?
Any product containing nicotine can be dangerous to a child or pet. Liquids are concentrated, and pouches can look like sweets. Treat all of them with the same care.

### Do child-resistant caps solve the problem?
They help but are not foolproof. Children can learn to open them, and caps can be left loose. Storage out of reach is the real protection.

### What if my pet chews a device?
Contact a veterinarian immediately, and tell them the product type and what was chewed. A damaged battery is also a hazard.

### How do I explain this to older children?
Be honest and clear: the products are for adults, they contain a substance that can harm young people and they must never be shared.

### What if I find a vape that is not mine?
Do not use it. Keep it away from children, and dispose of it responsibly.

## Browse
See [vape juice](/shop/vape-juice/) and [disposable vapes](/shop/disposables/). All products are for adults aged 21 and over, and nicotine is addictive. If you have any concern about exposure, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 or emergency services.

## A home audit in ten minutes
Walk through your home with a child's eye view. Check low shelves, coffee tables, bedside tables, bags on the floor and coat pockets. Check where you charge devices. Check your car's glove box and door pockets. Move everything to a high, closed, lockable place. Put a small box in each room where you tend to vape, so that you can put products away immediately. Tell everyone in the household where products are kept, and agree that they never leave them out. A ten-minute check, done every few months, keeps your habits honest.

## Teaching and talking
Children are curious, and curiosity is natural. Simple, calm rules work better than long lectures: these things are for adults only, they can hurt you and you must tell a grown-up if you find one. If a child finds a product, praise them for telling you, instead of scolding. For teenagers, honest conversation about nicotine and addiction is more effective than a ban alone, and a healthcare professional can help if you are worried about a young person using these products.

## Pets
Pets explore with their noses and mouths, and they can reach more than you expect. Cats jump onto shelves, dogs chew bags and small animals can be harmed by amounts that would not bother a person. Keep products where pets cannot reach, including in bags on the floor. If you vape indoors, be aware that residue can settle on surfaces, and clean them regularly.

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Is vapor around children a concern?
Avoid vaping around children and pets, and keep vapor away from them. If you vape indoors, ventilate and clean surfaces, because residue can settle.

### Are pouches as risky as liquids?
Pouches contain nicotine and can look like sweets. Keep the can closed and out of reach, and dispose of used pouches where children and pets cannot reach them.

### Should I tell my doctor or vet about exposure?
Yes. Call Poison Control or emergency services first, and then follow professional advice. Tell the vet what product was involved and the amount, if you know it.

## Planning for emergencies in advance
Save the Poison Control number, 1-800-222-1222, in your phone and write it where family members can see it, for example on the fridge or inside a cabinet door. Know the name and address of a nearby veterinary emergency clinic. Teach other adults in the household what to do: call first, have the packaging ready and do not wait for symptoms. A prepared household reacts faster, and in an exposure, speed matters.

## Keep a record of what you have
It helps to know how many bottles, devices and cans you have, so that you can tell at once if something is missing. After guests visit, check that nothing has been moved or left out. If you find a product somewhere unexpected, find out how it got there and fix the cause. A little awareness goes a long way in keeping products where they belong.

faq.q: Why is e-liquid dangerous to children and pets?
faq.a: It contains nicotine, and a small amount can harm a child or small pet. It can be swallowed or absorbed through the skin.

faq.q: Where should I store vapes and liquids?
faq.a: In a high, closed cabinet or a lockable box, out of reach and out of sight, not on tables, in handbags or in cars.

faq.q: Should I keep the original packaging?
faq.a: Yes. Child-resistant caps and labels matter, and the packaging helps Poison Control identify the contents. Do not decant liquid into food-style containers.

faq.q: What should I do if someone is exposed?
faq.a: Contact Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 in the U.S., or your local emergency number, right away. For pets, call a veterinarian.

faq.q: How do I handle spills?
faq.a: Wipe with paper towels while wearing gloves, wash the surface and your hands, and dispose of the towels responsibly.

faq.q: Can anyone under 21 handle a vape?
faq.a: No. Never let anyone under 21 handle a vape.

title: What the Nicotine Warning Label Means
summary: Every nicotine product carries a warning. Here is what the statement says, why it is required and how to read it as an adult consumer.
body:
Look at any vape, e-liquid or pouch sold in the United States and you will find a warning: "WARNING: This product contains nicotine. Nicotine is an addictive chemical." It is short, it appears on every package, and it is easy to skim past. This guide explains what the warning is, why it exists, what it tells you, where to find it, what it does not say, what other warnings you may see and why we repeat it throughout our site. It is general information, not legal advice or medical advice. Laws change and differ by state and city, so check the rules where you live. Everything we sell is for adults aged 21 and over, and nicotine is addictive.

## Why the warning exists
The FDA requires the warning on the packaging and in advertisements for nicotine products. It must be clear, prominent and in a set format. It exists to remind adults that nicotine is addictive, and it applies whatever the brand, the flavor or the type of device. When you see it, it is a reminder that these products carry a real risk of dependence, and that they are intended only for adults.

## What it tells you
Nicotine is a stimulant that the body can become dependent on. Using a product that contains it can lead to cravings and dependence, which is why products are limited to adults aged 21 and over. The word "addictive" is not a figure of speech: it means that regular use can make it hard to stop, and that stopping may cause withdrawal symptoms. The warning does not tell you how addictive a particular product is, or compare it with other products. It tells you that the substance is addictive.

### What dependence can feel like
People describe dependence as strong cravings, irritability, difficulty concentrating, restlessness or a feeling that they need a product to feel normal. These experiences differ from person to person. If you recognize them, or if you worry about your use, speak to a healthcare professional. We cannot give medical advice, and nothing here is medical advice.

## Where to find it
On the front or side panel of the package, often in a bordered box, and in advertisements and on websites that sell the product. On a disposable, it is on the box and often on the device. On a bottle, it is on the label. On a can of pouches, it is on the lid or side. You will also see it on our site, at the age gate, in the announcement bar and on product pages. If a product has no warning, treat it with caution and do not buy it. A missing or reworded warning can be a sign that the product does not meet the rules, or that it is not genuine. See [how to spot counterfeit vapes](/blog/how-to-spot-counterfeit-vapes/).

## What it does not say
It does not describe a product as more or less harmful than any other. It makes no comparison between nicotine products and anything else. We do not make health comparisons, and neither should sellers. If a seller makes claims about health benefits or about being less risky, be cautious, because such claims are tightly regulated. See [the FDA and vaping products](/blog/fda-and-vaping-products-what-adults-should-know/).

## Other warnings you may see
You may see notes for pregnant or nursing women, for people with health conditions and for children and pets. Follow them. Typical statements include that products are not for use by anyone under 21, that they should be kept out of reach of children and pets and that anyone with a medical condition or taking medication should ask a professional before use. These are separate from the nicotine warning, and they come from the manufacturer or from local rules. Nothing here is medical advice; consult a healthcare professional with questions.

### State and local warnings
Some states require additional notices, such as signs in shops or specific statements on products. If you live in such a state, you may see more text than the federal statement. These do not replace the federal warning; they add to it.

## How we use the warning
We show the warning where it matters: at our age gate, in our site banner, on product pages and in our policies. We do so because it is required, and because it is the right thing to do. Repeating it is not a formality. It is a reminder that every product on this site contains nicotine, is for adults only and carries a risk of dependence. Read our [FDA disclaimer](/fda-disclaimer/) and [terms](/terms/) for more.

## Reading the label as a whole
The warning is one part of a label. A good habit is to read the whole label before you use a product: the strength, the volume, the ingredients where listed, the manufacturer's details, the instructions and the warnings. If any of these is missing or looks wrong, ask us before you use it. See [how to read an e-liquid label](/blog/how-to-read-an-e-liquid-label/) and [nicotine strength guide](/blog/nicotine-strength-guide/).

## Common questions
### Does the warning apply to nicotine pouches?
Yes. Products that contain nicotine carry the warning, including pouches, liquids and devices.

### Does a zero-nicotine product need the warning?
Products labelled as containing no nicotine may carry different notices. Check the label. We label zero-nicotine products clearly on the product page.

### Why is the warning so blunt?
Because it is meant to be clear. A direct statement is easier to understand and harder to ignore than a long explanation.

### Can a seller remove or hide it?
No. Removing or hiding the warning is against the rules. If a product arrives without one, contact us.

### Does the warning mean I should not use the product?
It means you should understand the risk before you use it. These products are for adults who choose to use nicotine, and anyone with concerns should speak to a healthcare professional.

## Related
See the [FDA overview](/blog/fda-and-vaping-products-what-adults-should-know/) and our [FDA disclaimer](/fda-disclaimer/). Learn about [nicotine strength](/blog/nicotine-strength-guide/). Browse [disposable vapes](/shop/disposables/). All products are for adults aged 21 and over, and nicotine is addictive.

## Why the wording is so plain
The warning is written in simple words so that anyone can understand it at a glance, in the seconds a person spends looking at a package. It states two facts: the product contains nicotine, and nicotine is addictive. It does not hedge, and it does not tell a story. That directness is the point. If you remember only one thing from a label, it should be this.

## A worked example: reading a bottle
You pick up a bottle of e-liquid. On the front, you see the brand and the flavor. On the side, in a box, you see the warning. On the back, you see the strength, the volume, the ratio and the manufacturer's details. You read the warning, check that the strength is what you intended and look at the volume. You now know what you are buying, and that it is for adults only. If any part of the label were missing, you would ask the seller before using the product.

## Talking about the warning with others
If someone you know uses nicotine products, the warning is a neutral starting point for a conversation, not an accusation. It says the same thing to everyone: nicotine is addictive. If a friend or relative wants to cut down or stop, they can speak to a healthcare professional about the support that is available. If you are a parent, the warning is a good reason to keep products locked away and to talk to older children about why they are for adults only.

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Does the warning change with strength?
The statement is the same regardless of strength. The strength is shown separately on the label, and our [nicotine strength guide](/blog/nicotine-strength-guide/) explains how to read it.

### Who enforces the warning rule?
Federal regulators enforce labeling requirements, and sellers that ignore them can face action. As a buyer, your role is to read the label and to be cautious of products without one.

### Do ads need the warning too?
Yes. Advertisements for nicotine products must carry the statement, which is why you see it on product pages and in our site banner.

### Can the warning be in another language?
The required statement must be in English on products for the U.S. market. Packaging only in another language is a concern, because it may not have been made for this market.

## Using the warning as a check on products
The warning can also serve as a quick quality check. When you receive a product, look for the statement in the right place, in clear English, in the right words. If it is missing, faded, misspelled or different from the standard wording, ask the seller. Properly labelled products are a sign that the maker and the seller follow the rules, and unlabelled ones are a sign that something may be wrong. Take the extra few seconds on every new product.

## Why we mention it so often
You will see the statement on our age gate, in our banner and across our site. That repetition is deliberate. We would rather remind you too often than too rarely, because the message is simple and important: these products contain nicotine, nicotine is addictive and they are for adults aged 21 and over.

faq.q: What is the nicotine warning?
faq.a: "WARNING: This product contains nicotine. Nicotine is an addictive chemical." The FDA requires it on packaging and advertisements for nicotine products.

faq.q: Why is it there?
faq.a: To remind adults that nicotine is addictive, which is also why products are limited to adults aged 21 and over.

faq.q: Where do I find it?
faq.a: On the front or side panel of the package, often in a bordered box, and on advertisements and product pages.

faq.q: What if a product has no warning?
faq.a: Treat it with caution and do not buy it. A missing or reworded warning can be a sign that the product does not meet the rules.

faq.q: Does it compare products?
faq.a: No. It does not describe a product as more or less harmful than any other. We do not make health comparisons.

faq.q: Is this medical advice?
faq.a: No. Consult a healthcare professional with questions about nicotine and your health.
